\section{What carries the shortcut decides the fix}\label{sec:guide}\label{sec:solution}
The location law says what masking cannot do; it does not by itself say what to do instead. We evaluated the
mitigation families that a practitioner can apply to a frozen encoder, grouped by the supervision they need
(Table~\ref{m:tab:remedies}; full results, methods and ablations in Supplement~S8). Three regimes emerge, and the
linear-Gaussian account (Sec.~\ref{sec:theory}) explains each.

\input{tables/main_inroi_compact}

\paragraph{(1) Distinct overlays that carry the shortcut in their pixels} Sonographer calipers and synthetic rulers,
debris and tubes. Masking removes an out-of-ROI copy and leaves an in-ROI copy. Without any
artifact annotation, erasing from the frozen features the subspace along which \emph{generic} synthetic overlays move
the representation of masked images (mask-then-erase, U-MtE; Supplement~S8) removes most of what masking leaves:
thyroid $+0.224$ [$+0.195, +0.253$] over masking with DINOv2, $+0.246$ [$+0.224, +0.269$] with MedSigLIP and
$+0.135$ [$+0.102, +0.168$] with a ConvNeXt, and erasure beats augmentation with the same overlays (thyroid $+0.215$
[$+0.189, +0.244$]). With image-level artifact labels, group balancing on top of it is the most robust option
(Table~\ref{m:tab:remedies}).

\paragraph{(2) Artifacts that resemble the pathology} Capsule debris versus erosion fibrin. Any subspace estimated
from artifact appearance also contains disease evidence ($\rho$ large in Sec.~\ref{sec:theory}); unprotected erasure
is worse than masking ($-0.126$ [$-0.146, -0.107$]), protecting the label directions removes the failure but not the shortcut
($-0.006$ [$-0.018, +0.006$]). With image-level artifact labels masking plus last-layer retraining is the most robust
option (0.88).

\paragraph{(3) Shortcuts carried by correlates of the artifact} Dermoscopic hair co-varies with body site, age and
sex; a chest drain comes with a treated lung. Removing every hair patch with an oracle mask gains only $+0.015$;
no pixel- or insertion-based method closes the gap, and label-based reweighting (DFR, group balancing) is required.
The oracle-removal ceiling on a handful of annotated images diagnoses this regime.

\paragraph{Remedies do not transfer to unaltered test data} The regimes above are defined on the traps, whose reversed
test sets are extreme by construction. On the unaltered test distributions (Sec.~\ref{sec:natural}) no remedy is
uniformly better than the unmasked model: \input{tables/review2_guide_natural}. On the shortcut-conflicting pairs,
however, label-based group balancing does help: over masking $+0.136$ [$+0.063, +0.207$] on the thyroid split, $+0.043$
[$+0.026, +0.059$] and $+0.100$ [$+0.055, +0.144$] for the BCN and MSK hold-outs and $+0.072$ [$+0.048, +0.097$] on
ISIC 2020, with no change for HAM and capsule; it costs overall AUROC on HAM ($-0.032$ [$-0.049, -0.013$]) and
capsule.
\paragraph{Is there one remedy to use instead of masking? (pre-registered)} We registered a criterion for
\emph{dominating} masking: not worse (margin 0.01) on the six unaltered test sets and on Trap~B and clean tests, better on
every Trap~A and on the conflicting pairs of the unaltered test sets, and no shortcut flipping --- 42 components, all of
which must hold (Supplement~S17). Settings were chosen on validation data only; confirmation used trap resamples generated
after each registration and one cohort (ovary) that never influenced a choice. In a first round no candidate dominated.
The closest, a class-conditional mean constraint on the masked features (the head may not score images with and without
the artifact differently within a class; an adaptation of counterfactual invariance, \citealp{veitch2021counterfactual}),
met 40 of 42 components: it is better than masking in every Trap~A (thyroid $+0.330$ [$+0.311, +0.351$], held-out ovary
$+0.118$ [$+0.089, +0.147$]) and on the conflicting pairs of every unaltered test set (ISIC 2020 $+0.078$
[$+0.069, +0.088$]), and equal elsewhere, but loses $-0.021$ [$-0.027, -0.016$] overall on ISIC 2020, where in-lesion hair
still helps most patients. A documented search over twelve further ideas (backdoor adjustment, product of experts, logit
adjustment, conditional adversarial debiasing, contrastive and invariance methods) on development data, and a second
registered round of its three best on new data, gave the same result: IRMv1 met 41 of 42 components and lost only on ISIC
2020 overall ($-0.009$ [$-0.013, -0.005$]); the first round's constraint, refitted, replicated its result. Every
alternative to masking, including the unmasked model, loses overall on ISIC 2020 ($-0.009$ to $-0.029$), mostly on pairs
whose images share the artifact status: there masking is simply the better disease ranker.

We therefore offer the regimes as a decision guide for \emph{auditing} a model, not as a claim that any remedy
improves deployment performance everywhere; where artifacts may lie inside the ROI, the class-conditional constraint is the
registered option that fixes masking's failure at the smallest measured cost:
(i) measure where artifacts sit relative to the ROI; out-of-ROI artifacts are what masking removes;
(ii) for in-ROI artifacts estimate which regime applies (oracle-removal ceiling, resemblance to the pathology);
(iii) evaluate any mitigation on shortcut-conflicting cases \emph{and} on the unaltered distribution, reporting clean,
correlated and reversed performance together, because a reversed-environment gain can be manufactured by removing
diagnosis signal (Supplement~S8).
